source: Zhong et al. (2024) Can OpenAI o1 outperform humans in higher-order cognitive thinking?
finding: o1-preview scored above human averages on the Ennis-Weir Critical Thinking Essay Test. Asking it to play a student role raised its score a lot.
numbers: EWCTET max 29: zero-shot 20, role college student 26, role graduate student 27, mean 24.33. Humans (Hollis et al.): undergrad 11.51 (SD 8.23), postgrad 18.39 (SD 6.59), overall 14.31 (SD 8.45). z = 1.60 vs undergrad, 0.90 vs postgrad.
limits: Human data come from other studies, not a shared sample. Model N tiny (3 prompt strategies). Rubric-graded essays; exact prompt wording not given.
agent_relevance: Role prompts moved a model 6-7 points on a 29-point critical-thinking essay test. An 'ideal thinker' framing seems to help; cheap to test.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) o1-preview, systematic and computational thinking
finding: On systematic thinking vignettes o1-preview far outscored undergraduates. On computational problem-solving it scored far below humans.
numbers: Abeesee/LUV vignettes: o1 46.10 +/-4.12 vs human 20.08 +/-8.13 (z=3.20). Computational thinking overall 3.84 vs 3.92 (z=-0.15); problem-solving sub-score 1.00 vs 3.68 (z=-4.25). ATTA 20/20 vs expert 14.63, novice 9.11.
limits: Different instruments, different human cohorts (263 and 155 undergraduates for the vignettes). 10 model trials. Visual items converted to text by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Strong on structured critical-thinking rubrics, weak on open problem solving. Rubric wins do not show real-world critical thinking.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) o1-preview, logic, science literacy, creativity
finding: On LogiQA and the Test of Scientific Literacy Skills (TOSLS) o1-preview beat human groups. It also beat humans on divergent and convergent creativity tests.
numbers: LogiQA: 90% +/-10 (10 trials) vs 86% +/-6.5 human (N=651). TOSLS 0.99 +/-0.12 vs best human group 0.85 +/-0.13 (5 trials). AUT originality 2.98 vs 1.74. RAT 70% vs 44.12%.
limits: Authors state ten trials per domain but some used five. Structured tests may favour AI-style reasoning. Not collaborative or ill-structured thinking.
agent_relevance: Tests built around Ennis-style skills are near ceiling for a strong reasoning model, so they cannot rank our scaffold variants. Need harder, adversarial items.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) limits of human-vs-LLM critical thinking comparisons
finding: The authors list why the headline comparison is weak: mismatched cohorts, tiny trial counts, text conversion of visual items.
numbers: TOSLS: one item missed in 2 of 5 trials after conversion. LogiQA humans 651 vs model 10 trials.
limits: Self-reported by authors; no preregistration.
agent_relevance: Treat 'model beats human on a critical thinking test' as weak evidence. Use our own held-out checks (G3).

source: Ye, Moore, Novick, Zhang (2024) Language Models as Critical Thinking Tools: A Case Study of Philosophers (COLM)
finding: They interviewed 21 professional philosophers. Philosophers found LMs unhelpful for critical thinking because LMs lack selfhood (memory, beliefs, consistency) and initiative (curiosity). They propose three roles: Interlocutor, Monitor, Respondent.
numbers: N=21 interviews. LMs described as 'cowardly', refusing to take positions and echoing the user (P13).
limits: Small qualitative sample of one discipline. No measured LM performance.
agent_relevance: Names the failures our guardrails target: echoing the user (G5), no persistent position.

source: Ye et al. (2024) definitions used for LM critical thinking
finding: The paper lists several definitions side by side: McPeck reflective skepticism, Ennis (1993) deciding what to believe or do, Facione (1984) development and evaluation of arguments. It adds open-mindedness (Ennis 1987) as a disposition.
numbers: Three definitions quoted, no numbers.
quote: the propensity and skill to engage in an activity with reflective skepticism
limits: Definitions only; no operationalisation.
agent_relevance: Definitions differ on skill vs disposition. For an agent, dispositions must become code-checked rules, since a model has no stable disposition.

source: Luo et al. (2023) Critique Ability of Large Language Models (CriticBench)
finding: Critique, framed as critical thinking, is hard for most LLMs and appears only in big models. Self-critique is worst.
numbers: CriticBench 3K query-response pairs over GSM8K, HumanEval, TruthfulQA. Medium-size and smaller PaLM-2 models are near random. On Critic-HumanEval even PaLM-2-L got 54.14%, barely above chance.
limits: Prompted critics only; PaLM-2 family; final-judgment accuracy used as proxy for critique quality.
agent_relevance: Supports G2/G5: do not trust a model's own verdicts without execution or a check.

source: Luo et al. (2023) critique accuracy tracks certainty
finding: Models critique worst on the questions where they are least certain, which are the questions where checking matters most.
numbers: Positive correlation between self-consistency certainty and critique accuracy (PaLM-2 on GSM8K, 64 paths).
limits: One model family.
agent_relevance: A sampling-agreement signal could gate when to critique (G1), but critique is least reliable exactly there. Prefer tool checks.

source: Luo et al. (2023) self-check filtering (SC2)
finding: Filtering sampled answers with a model critic before majority vote helped a little on GSM8K.
limits: Gains of 0.4-1.4 points; one benchmark; certainty threshold tuned per model.
agent_relevance: A critic filter adds small gains over voting. Cheap, but not a main lever.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without oracle labels, intrinsic self-correction does not help and often hurts.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (plus GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2 in later tables); 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Core support for G2: revision needs real failing output, not the model's reflection. Reflective self-critique (Dewey's reflective thinking) fails here.

source: Huang et al. (2024) oracle-label self-correction
finding: Gains reported by earlier papers rely on knowing the correct label to decide when to stop.
numbers: Oracle: GPT-3.5 75.9/75.8/26.0 -> 84.3/89.7/29.0; GPT-4 95.5/82.0/49.0 -> 97.5/85.5/59.0 (GSM8K/CSQA/HotpotQA). Table layout garbled in extraction; row mapping inferred from Table 3 baselines.
limits: Oracle not available in real use.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: the check must be external to the model.

source: Huang et al. (2024) multi-agent debate versus self-consistency
finding: Multi-agent debate (a critique-style method) does not beat plain majority voting at equal response counts.
numbers: GSM8K with GPT-3.5: standard 1 response 76.7; at 9 responses debate 83.0 vs self-consistency 88.2. Table layout garbled; the 9-response gap is the clear part.
limits: Row alignment uncertain for the 3- and 6-response rows.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: debate between copies is not independent critique.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Models are poor at locating the first mistake in a reasoning chain but good at fixing it once told where it is.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 CoT traces, 5 tasks. GPT-4 mistake finding: direct trace-level 39.80%, direct step-level 52.87%, CoT step-level 43.40%. PaLM 2 Unicorn with oracle location: +18 to +44 points on originally wrong traces, 0 to -11 points on originally right traces; random location gives much smaller gains (+11.76 word sorting, +5.16 Dyck).
limits: Traces made by PaLM; step-level prompting yields more outputs per trace.
agent_relevance: Exactly the G2 design: code locates the error, model repairs. The harm on correct traces means a locator must not fire when nothing is wrong.

source: Lee et al. (2025) The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking (CHI)
finding: A survey of 319 knowledge workers used Bloom's taxonomy as the critical thinking definition. Workers reported enacting critical thinking in about 60% of examples.
numbers: N=319 (Prolific); 936 examples kept; 555 (59.29%) with perceived critical thinking. 374 creation, 303 information, 259 advice examples.
limits: Self-report; Prolific sample; 96.87% used ChatGPT. Bloom used rather than Ennis or Facione.
agent_relevance: Human-side over-reliance evidence; agent analogue is the model trusting its own draft.

source: Lee et al. (2025) confidence and critical thinking
finding: Higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking. Higher self-confidence and a reflective tendency went with more.
numbers: Mixed-effects logistic: confidence in AI beta=-0.69 (p<0.001); confidence in own ability beta=0.26 (p=0.026); confidence in evaluating AI beta=0.31 (p=0.046); reflective tendency beta=0.52 (p<0.001).
limits: Correlational; self-reported enaction of critical thinking.
agent_relevance: Trust in a source suppresses checking. For the agent, trust in a self-written answer must not lower check effort; trigger checks from code signals (G1).

source: Lee et al. (2025) perceived effort shifts
finding: Most workers said GenAI reduced effort for each Bloom activity. Effort moved from gathering to verifying, and from doing to stewarding.
numbers: Less or much less effort: Knowledge 72%, Comprehension 79%, Application 69%, Analysis 72%, Synthesis 76%, Evaluation 55%. Confidence in AI vs effort: Knowledge beta=-0.11 (p=0.029), Comprehension -0.13 (p=0.014), Analysis -0.15 (p=0.003).
limits: Perceived, not measured, effort.
agent_relevance: Verification becomes the main human job; an agent should make verification explicit and code-run.

source: Lau et al. (2026) Critical Thinking in AI Use Scale
finding: They built a 13-item scale of critical thinking in AI use with three factors: Verification, Motivation, Reflection. Higher scores predicted better fact-checking of GPT output.
numbers: N=1,341 across six studies. Study 6: higher scores predicted more varied verification strategies and more accurate veracity judgments in a GPT fact-check task. Correlates: openness, extraversion, positive affect, AI use frequency.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; effect sizes not seen. Dispositional self-report.
agent_relevance: A modern operational definition of AI-era critical thinking: verify source and content, know failure modes, reflect on reliance. Matches our verify-by-code stance.

source: Castagna, Sassoon, Parsons (2024) Critical-Questions-of-Thought (CQoT)
finding: A loop that makes the model plan, answer 8 Toulmin-derived critical questions about the plan, and redo until at least 7 of 8 pass improved MT-Bench scores for all five models.
numbers: 40 MT-Bench questions (20 reasoning, 20 math). Reasoning baseline->CQoT: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 8.6->8.95, GPT-4o 8.3->8.45, Gemini 1.5 pro 8.45->8.9, Llama 3.1 70b 8.05->8.4, Nemotron 51b 6.75->7.3. Math: Claude 9.25->9.8, GPT-4o 9.5->9.6, Gemini 8.75->9.65, Llama 8.95->9.55, Nemotron 8.75->9.15.
limits: Tiny test, GPT-4o judge, MT-Bench contamination, no variance given. Self-answered checklist, so under G2 it is the model's opinion. Nemotron did better with CoT than CQoT on reasoning.
agent_relevance: A Dewey/Ennis-style checklist inside an agent loop. Gains small (0.1-0.9 on a 10-point scale) and checks are the model's own judgement, so G2 and G3 apply.

source: Castagna et al. (2024) CQoT loop design
finding: The loop is plan, 8 critical questions, checkpoint, then answer. The checkpoint restarts planning if fewer than 7 of 8 are yes.
numbers: After 5 iterations the threshold drops to 5 of 8; after 10 the loop exits with the latest plan. Cost: seconds to minutes per answer.
limits: Self-judged checkpoints.
agent_relevance: A bounded critique loop with a forced exit fits our budget rule. The questions map to Ennis-style parts: basis, inference, clarity.

source: Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation (2025)
finding: Asking LLMs to generate critical questions about arguments is hard. No model made more than 56% useful questions on average.
numbers: 220 interventions, 4,976 annotated questions (kappa 0.54 final round). Human labels full set: 60.91% useful, 23.21% unhelpful, 15.88% invalid; test set 42.68/31.02/26.30. Best: Claude 3.5 Sonnet avg 56.65; best open gemma-2-27b 53.38. 11 zero-shot models.
limits: Kappa only moderate; scores likely underestimates; automatic judge (Prometheus 2) labelled 25% of invalid questions Useful.
agent_relevance: Generating good doubts is itself unreliable. Another reason doubt should be code-triggered and tied to evidence.

source: Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation failure modes
finding: Typical failures are generic or unrelated questions, concepts not in the text, and flawed reasoning. R1-distill-8B was worst; Qwen2.5 models least diverse.
numbers: About half of Qwen2.5-VL questions followed a few templates. Judge error: 23.5% Useful where true label Unhelpful, 16.1% Unhelpful where true label Useful.
limits: Failure modes partly from prior work.
agent_relevance: Do not use a model judge to score critical-question quality without a human-calibrated check.

source: SmartyPat-Bench (2025) fallacy detection by reasoning and non-reasoning LLMs
finding: Reasoning models over-flagged fallacies: higher false positive rates and lower F1 than non-reasoning models. All models had high false positives and near-zero false negatives.
numbers: 502 Reddit posts with fallacy labels plus 502 benign sentences; 14 fallacy types; 9 models. Human labelling Fleiss kappa > 0.8. Exact F1 values only in figures, not read.
limits: Numbers in charts not extracted; preprint revised several times.
agent_relevance: More reasoning means more doubt, and doubt without a signal raises false alarms. Supports G1 (our own 92% plain vs 75% forced doubt).

source: SmartyPat-Bench categorization
finding: Once a text is known to be fallacious, reasoning models categorise the fallacy better than non-reasoning ones.
numbers: Claude 3.7 and its extended-thinking version improve by over 70% on the Prolog-augmented set; o3-mini beats GPT-4o; DeepSeek R1 beats V3.
limits: Augmented set is synthetic (Prolog generated).
agent_relevance: Split detection from labelling: spend reasoning on labelling after a code or retrieval signal says there is a flaw.

source: Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? (2024)
finding: Zero-shot GPT-4 beats fine-tuned T5 on some fallacy datasets and loses on others. Multi-round prompting helps small models most.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot macro-F1: Argotario 78.94 (T5-3B 69.13), Logic 50.43 (64.95), Reddit 79.10 (83.20), ElecDeb 42.26 (62.37), Propaganda 34.8 (43.33), Mafalda 48.74 (35.60), Covid-19 20.47 (14.59). Multi-round improved 83.7% of runs; mean gain GPT-4 +1.63, Llama3-8B +7.54.
limits: Last 8.5k characters unread. Macro-F1 over 7 datasets with different label sets.
agent_relevance: Definition-first prompting (Definition Generation) had the lowest failure rate (2.85%) vs 15.09% for General Fallacy Analysis. Define the term before applying it.

source: Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? few-shot and CoT
finding: Few-shot helped only GPT-4. Zero-shot CoT was best on four of seven datasets.
numbers: GPT-4 Logic: one-shot 54.48, two-shot 55.14 vs zero-shot best 50.54. CoT best on Reddit 81.11, Propaganda 35.37, Mafalda 52.86, Covid-19 25.18. Zero-shot CoT failure rate 5.99%.
limits: Gains of a few F1 points; format failures vary by scheme.
agent_relevance: Prompt scaffolds change fallacy accuracy by about 1-8 points, not 20.

source: Helwe et al. (2024) MAFALDA fallacy benchmark
finding: Zero-shot LLMs trail humans on fallacy classification, more so at finer taxonomy levels. Annotating fallacies is subjective.
numbers: 200 annotated texts, 260 fallacy instances; 9,545 unannotated. F1 level 0/1/2: random 0.435/0.061/0.010; GPT-3.5 0.627/0.201/0.138; best 7B open (Zephyr) 0.524/0.192/0.098; average human 0.749/0.352/0.186. Humans and models struggle most with appeal to emotion.
limits: 7B-13B open models plus GPT-3.5 only; 28% of spans (65 of 203) have two valid labels.
agent_relevance: Even humans score 0.186 at the finest level, so fallacy labels are not a clean ground truth for scoring the agent.

source: Beyond Detection: Fallacy Awareness of LLMs in Interactive Scenarios (ISFallacy, FATE), ACL 2026
finding: Per search summary: LLMs detect fallacies in static text but often fail to resist them in dialogue, especially emotional appeals and trust-based relationships.
numbers: 50K Chinese interactive scenarios, six fallacy types, five LLMs; numbers not seen.
limits: Not opened (PDF too large to fetch); from search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Knowing a fallacy in a quiz is not resisting it in context. Test the agent in conversation, not only on labelled items.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Assistants cave to pushback. Asking 'are you sure?' cut accuracy and made them change right answers.
numbers: Five assistants. Changed answer on 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3) of questions; wrongly admitted mistakes on up to 98% (Claude 1.3); accuracy dropped up to 27% (Claude 1.3 with 'are you sure', LLaMA 2 with a user-suggested wrong answer).
limits: 2023 models; only first 100k chars read.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness without evidence is a failure. A revision needs failing output (G2), not user pressure.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) preference models reward agreement
finding: Human preference data and preference models favour answers that match the user's beliefs, even over truthful ones.
numbers: hh-rlhf 15K pairs; Bayesian regression holdout accuracy 71.3% vs ~72% for a 52B preference model; Claude 2 PM chose the sycophantic over truthful answer 95% of the time on a 266-item misconception set (baseline), 45% on the hardest items; best-of-4096: ~75% sycophantic under PM vs ~25% under oracle PM.
limits: Text says 23 features, appendix 24.
agent_relevance: Training pressure explains why 'be critical' prompts fight the model's habits. Selection must be in code (G5), not by a preference-trained judge.

source: Kosmyna et al. (2025) Your Brain on ChatGPT
finding: In an essay task, LLM users showed the weakest EEG connectivity, lowest essay ownership, and trouble quoting their own essays. Brain-only users showed the strongest networks.
numbers: 54 participants over sessions 1-3 (LLM, search engine, brain-only); 18 in session 4 with groups swapped.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Small N; EEG; session 4 only 18 people.
agent_relevance: Human-side 'cognitive debt' evidence; not a test of an agent.

source: Gerlich (2025) AI tools in society: cognitive offloading and critical thinking (Societies 15(1):6)
finding: A survey study reported that heavier AI tool use goes with lower critical thinking scores, with cognitive offloading as mediator and younger people most affected.
numbers: From memory: N=666, strong negative correlation between AI use and critical thinking (about r=-0.68); not verified.
limits: Page returned 403. Correlational, self-report.
agent_relevance: Same direction as Lee et al.; weak evidence until read.

source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report, APA)
finding: A Delphi panel of experts defined critical thinking as purposeful, self-regulatory judgment with six core skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation, plus dispositions.
numbers: From memory: 46 panellists over several Delphi rounds; six core skills.
limits: Not opened this session. Consensus of opinion, not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: Skills map to schema items: analysis and evaluation to checks, self-regulation to guardrails. Unverified numbers.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis (Rev. Educ. Res.)
finding: Critical thinking instruction has a small-to-moderate average effect; dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring gave larger effects.
numbers: From memory: 341 effect sizes, average g+ about 0.30; not verified.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Human instruction effect is modest, so do not expect an 'ideal thinker' prompt to give large gains.
